decks.title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure — Part 1: Lewis structures, bond parameters and polarity
goals: Explain the octet rule, ionic bonding and lattice enthalpy qualitatively
Draw Lewis structures and calculate formal charges, including resonance and octet exceptions
Use bond length, bond angle, bond enthalpy and bond order to compare bonds
Explain bond polarity and dipole moment, including NH₃ and NF₃, H₂O and CO₂, and BF₃

slides.heading: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
slides.body_md: Part 1 — why atoms join, how to draw their bonding electrons, and what the measurable properties of a bond tell us.

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of chemical bond with how each forms and examples

slides.narration: Almost nothing around us is a free atom. Atoms combine, and the way they combine decides whether a substance is a salt, a gas or a liquid. In this part we meet the Kössel and Lewis idea of the octet, draw Lewis structures, calculate formal charges, and use bond length, bond enthalpy and dipole moment to compare bonds.

slides.heading: The Kössel–Lewis approach and the octet rule
slides.body_md: Atoms combine to reach the **stable configuration of a noble gas**: eight electrons in the outer shell (the **octet**), or two for hydrogen (the **duplet**). A **Lewis symbol** shows the valence electrons as dots around the atomic symbol.

visual.alt: Table of the number of valence electrons in each main group with an example element

slides.narration: Kössel and Lewis explained bonding by the unusual stability of the noble gases. An atom tends to gain, lose or share electrons until it has eight in its outer shell, an octet. Hydrogen needs only two. A Lewis symbol is just the atom’s symbol with dots for its valence electrons, and the number of dots equals the group number, or the group number minus ten for the p block.

slides.heading: Ionic bonds and lattice enthalpy
slides.body_md: An ionic bond forms when a metal **loses** and a non-metal **gains** electrons, and the ions attract. It is favoured by a **low ionisation enthalpy** of the metal, a **negative electron gain enthalpy** of the non-metal and a **high lattice enthalpy**. Lattice enthalpy rises with **higher ionic charge** and **smaller ionic size**.

visual.alt: Table of approximate lattice enthalpies of four ionic compounds rising with smaller ions and higher charge

slides.narration: Lattice enthalpy is the energy released when separated gaseous ions come together to make the crystal. It is the main source of the stability of an ionic solid. It is larger when the ions are small, because they get closer, and when the charges are high. That is why magnesium oxide, with doubly charged ions, has a lattice enthalpy several times that of sodium chloride.

slides.heading: Covalent bonds and Lewis structures
slides.body_md: In a **covalent bond** atoms **share** electron pairs: one pair for a single bond, two for a double bond, three for a triple bond. To draw a Lewis structure, count the valence electrons (add one per negative charge), arrange the atoms, give each an octet and check the formal charges.

nodes.label: Skeleton: least electronegative atom in the centre
Multiple bonds if electrons are short

visual.alt: Flow of five steps for drawing a Lewis structure

slides.narration: Here is a method that works for most molecules and ions. Count all the valence electrons, adding one for each negative charge and removing one for each positive charge. Put the least electronegative atom in the centre, join atoms with single bonds, and place the remaining electrons as lone pairs to complete octets. If electrons are short, use double or triple bonds. Finally check formal charges.

slides.heading: Worked example: the nitrate ion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Draw the Lewis structure of $\ce{NO3-}$ and find the formal charge on each atom.

**Step 1.** Valence electrons: $5 + 3 \times 6 + 1 = 24$.

**Step 2.** N in the centre with three O atoms; one N=O double bond and two N–O⁻ single bonds so that every atom has an octet.

**Step 3.** Formal charge $=$ V − L − B/2: N $= 5 - 0 - 4 = +1$; double-bonded O $= 6 - 4 - 2 = 0$; each single-bonded O $= 6 - 6 - 1 = −1$.

**Check.** $+1 + 0 + 2(-1) = -1$, the charge on the ion.

visual.alt: Table of the valence electrons, lone-pair electrons, half the bonding electrons and formal charge of each atom in the nitrate ion

slides.narration: Nitrate has twenty four valence electrons: five from nitrogen, eighteen from three oxygens, and one for the negative charge. Put nitrogen in the middle with one double bond and two single bonds. Nitrogen then has formal charge plus one, the double bonded oxygen zero, and each single bonded oxygen minus one. The total is minus one, matching the ion.

slides.heading: Formal charge
slides.body_md: **Formal charge = V − L − B/2**, where V is the valence electrons of the free atom, L the non-bonding electrons and B the bonding electrons. The best Lewis structure has **the smallest formal charges**, with any negative charge on the **more electronegative** atom.

visual.alt: Table of formal charges on the three oxygen atoms of an ozone Lewis structure

slides.narration: Formal charge is a bookkeeping device. Pretend every bond is shared equally and ask how many electrons each atom owns compared with its free state. In ozone the central oxygen has a lone pair and three bonds, so plus one. One end oxygen is minus one and the other is zero. When there are several possible structures, choose the one with charges as small as possible.

slides.heading: Quick check: formal charge
slides.body_md: Calculate a formal charge from V, L and B.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write down the valence electrons, the lone pair electrons and the bonding electrons, then use the formula.

slides.heading: Exceptions to the octet rule
slides.body_md: **Incomplete octet:** fewer than eight around the central atom (BeCl₂ 4, BF₃ 6, AlCl₃ 6). **Odd-electron molecules:** NO and NO₂ have one unpaired electron. **Expanded octet:** period 3 and later atoms can hold more than eight using d orbitals (PCl₅ 10, SF₆ 12).

visual.alt: Table of five molecules that break the octet rule, with the electrons around the central atom

slides.narration: The octet rule has exceptions. Beryllium and boron compounds have fewer than eight electrons and look for partners, as boron trifluoride does when it takes a fluoride. Nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide have an odd number of electrons. And phosphorus pentachloride and sulfur hexafluoride have ten and twelve electrons, which is possible only because period three atoms have d orbitals.

slides.heading: Bond parameters
slides.body_md: **Bond length** is the distance between nuclei; **bond angle** is the angle between bonds at an atom; **bond enthalpy** is the energy to break one mole of bonds in the gas phase; **bond order** is the number of bonds between two atoms. For the same atoms, a **higher bond order gives a shorter, stronger bond**.

visual.alt: Table of bond order, bond length and bond enthalpy for five covalent bonds showing shorter and stronger bonds at higher bond order

slides.narration: Four quantities describe a bond. Length is the distance between the two nuclei, and the angle describes the geometry. Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break the bond, and bond order is the number of shared pairs. As the order goes up from carbon carbon single to triple, the bond becomes shorter and much stronger, as the table shows.

slides.heading: Resonance
slides.body_md: When one Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule, several **resonance structures** differing only in the position of electrons are drawn. The real molecule is a **resonance hybrid**, more stable than any one structure, with bonds of **equal length** and a **fractional bond order**.

visual.alt: Table of ozone, carbonate and nitrate with the number of resonance structures, the fractional bond order and the equal bond lengths

slides.narration: Experiment shows that both oxygen oxygen bonds in ozone are the same length, which one Lewis structure cannot explain, because it would show one single and one double bond. So we draw two structures and say the real molecule is a hybrid of both. In carbonate and nitrate, the double bond is shared among three positions, so each bond has order four thirds.

slides.heading: Worked example: comparing bond orders and lengths
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the bond order of the C–O bonds in $\ce{CO3^2-}$ and arrange O–O bonds in $\ce{O2}$, $\ce{O3}$ and $\ce{H2O2}$ by length.

**(a)** Carbonate: one C=O and two C–O⁻ shared over three equivalent bonds, so bond order $= \dfrac{2 + 1 + 1}{3} = 1.33$.

**(b)** O–O bond orders: $\ce{O2}$ 2, $\ce{O3}$ 1.5, $\ce{H2O2}$ 1. A higher bond order means a shorter bond: $\ce{O2}$ (121 pm) < $\ce{O3}$ (128 pm) < $\ce{H2O2}$ (148 pm).

visual.alt: Table of the O–O bond order and length in oxygen, ozone and hydrogen peroxide

slides.narration: For carbonate, add up the bonds, two plus one plus one, which is four, and share them over three positions to give four thirds. For the oxygen oxygen bonds, ranking by bond order is enough. Oxygen has order two, ozone one and a half, hydrogen peroxide one. The higher the order, the shorter the bond.

slides.heading: Quick check: resonance
slides.body_md: Find the bond order or the number of equal bonds in a resonance hybrid.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the total bonding pairs in one structure and divide by the number of equivalent bonds.

slides.heading: Bond polarity and dipole moment
slides.body_md: A bond between atoms of different **electronegativity** is polar. The **dipole moment** is $\mu = q \times d$, the charge times the distance, measured in debye (1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m). It is a **vector**, drawn from positive to negative.

visual.alt: Table of dipole moments of the hydrogen halides falling from hydrogen fluoride to hydrogen iodide as the halogen becomes less electronegative

slides.narration: A polar bond has a positive end and a negative end. The size of the effect is the dipole moment, equal to the charge times the distance between the charges. The hydrogen halides show the trend: as the halogen gets less electronegative from fluorine to iodine, the dipole moment falls steadily. The dipole moment is a vector with direction.

slides.heading: Dipole moments of molecules
slides.body_md: The molecular dipole moment is the **vector sum** of bond dipoles (and lone-pair dipoles). Symmetric molecules such as **CO₂, BF₃, CH₄** have **zero** moment. **H₂O** is bent, so its bond dipoles add. In **NH₃** the lone pair dipole **adds** to the N–H dipoles; in **NF₃** it **opposes** the N–F dipoles, so NF₃ has a much smaller moment.

rows: Two equal dipoles in opposite directions
Lone pair and N–H dipoles point the same way
Lone pair dipole opposes the N–F dipoles

visual.alt: Table of molecules with their shape, dipole moment and the reason for the value

slides.narration: Polar bonds do not always make a polar molecule, because dipoles are vectors. In carbon dioxide and boron trifluoride they cancel exactly. Water is bent, so they add. Ammonia and nitrogen trifluoride have the same shape, but in ammonia the lone pair points the same way as the bond dipoles, while in nitrogen trifluoride it opposes them, so its dipole moment is much smaller.

slides.heading: Worked example: percentage ionic character of HCl
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The dipole moment of HCl is 1.07 D and the bond length is 127 pm. Find the percentage ionic character. (1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m, e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

**Step 1.** $\mu = q \times d$, so $q = \dfrac{1.07 \times 3.336 \times 10^{-30}}{127 \times 10^{-12}} = 2.81 \times 10^{-20}\ \text{C}$.

**Step 2.** Fraction of a full charge: $\dfrac{2.81 \times 10^{-20}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} = 0.175$.

**Step 3.** Percentage ionic character $= 17.5\%$.

visual.alt: Table of the steps for finding the percentage ionic character of hydrogen chloride

slides.narration: Divide the dipole moment by the bond length to find the charge that is effectively separated. Then compare it with the charge of one electron. For hydrogen chloride, the separated charge is about one sixth of a full electron charge, so the bond is about seventeen and a half per cent ionic and mostly covalent.

slides.heading: Quick check: dipole moment
slides.body_md: Explain why two molecules of the same shape have different dipole moments.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about the direction of the lone pair dipole compared with the bond dipoles.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Octet rule (duplet for H); ionic bond: electron transfer, stability from lattice enthalpy (higher for small, highly charged ions).
Lewis structure steps; formal charge = V − L − B/2; the best structure has the smallest charges.
Exceptions: incomplete octet (BF₃), odd electron (NO), expanded octet (SF₆).
Bond order up means length down and enthalpy up; resonance gives fractional orders (O₃ 1.5; CO₃²⁻ and NO₃⁻ 1.33).
Dipole moment μ = q × d, a vector; CO₂, BF₃, CH₄ non-polar; NH₃ polar, NF₃ much less so.

visual.alt: Summary table of four key concepts of Part 1

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Atoms bond to reach an octet, by transferring electrons in ionic bonds or sharing them in covalent ones. We draw Lewis structures and use formal charge to choose the best. Some molecules break the octet rule. Bond order links length and strength, resonance gives fractional bond orders, and dipole moments are vectors that depend on shape as well as on bond polarity.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Show the formal-charge calculation with V, L and B/2, not just the answer.
For resonance, draw all the structures and state that the hybrid has equal bond lengths.
Say “vector sum” when explaining zero dipole moments of CO₂, BF₃ and CCl₄.
For NH₃ and NF₃, mention the direction of the lone-pair dipole.
Do not apply the octet rule to central atoms of period 3 or later without checking for expanded octets.

rows: Four thirds, shared over three bonds
CO₂ is polar because C=O is polar
Lattice enthalpy is the energy to form ions
It is the energy released when gaseous ions form the crystal

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. Always show the formal charge arithmetic. For resonance, draw every structure and say the hybrid has equal bonds. When explaining zero dipole moment, use the words vector sum. For ammonia versus nitrogen trifluoride, mention the direction of the lone pair dipole. And watch for expanded octets in period three.

decks.title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure — Part 2: Shapes, hybridisation, MO theory and hydrogen bonding
goals: Predict shapes of AB₂ to AB₆ molecules with and without lone pairs using VSEPR theory
Explain valence bond theory, σ and π bonds, and sp, sp², sp³, sp³d and sp³d² hybridisation
Build MO diagrams for H₂ to Ne₂ and deduce bond order and magnetic behaviour
Describe intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonding and its effects

slides.heading: Shapes of molecules and theories of bonding
slides.body_md: Part 2 — three models of molecules: VSEPR for shape, valence bond theory with hybridisation for bonding, and molecular orbital theory for magnetism and bond order.

visual.alt: Table linking the number of electron pairs to the arrangement and hybridisation

slides.narration: Lewis structures tell us which atoms are joined, but not the shape of a molecule. In this part we first predict shapes by counting electron pairs, with the VSEPR theory. Then we explain how bonds form by overlap of orbitals, using hybridisation, and finally we use molecular orbital theory to explain why oxygen is magnetic. We end with hydrogen bonding.

slides.heading: VSEPR theory
slides.body_md: Electron pairs around the central atom repel and take positions of **minimum repulsion**. Order of repulsion: **lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair**. A multiple bond counts as **one region** of electron density. The shape names only the **atoms**.

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of electron-pair repulsion in decreasing order of strength

slides.narration: The idea is simple. Electron pairs repel one another, so they spread as far apart as possible. A lone pair is held by only one nucleus, so it spreads out and repels more strongly than a bonding pair. That is why lone pairs squeeze bond angles. A double or triple bond counts as a single region, and the shape names only the positions of atoms, not the lone pairs.

slides.heading: Shapes with no lone pairs: AB₂ to AB₆
slides.body_md: With no lone pairs the shape matches the arrangement: **linear** (BeCl₂), **trigonal planar** (BF₃), **tetrahedral** (CH₄), **trigonal bipyramidal** (PCl₅; axial bonds are longer than equatorial) and **octahedral** (SF₆).

visual.caption: Schematic; solid lines are in or near the plane of the page, dashed lines point backwards.

slides.narration: Here are the five basic arrangements. Two pairs sit at one hundred and eighty degrees, three at one hundred and twenty, and four point to the corners of a tetrahedron at about one hundred and nine degrees. Five pairs form a trigonal bipyramid with two different kinds of position, axial and equatorial. Six pairs form an octahedron with all angles ninety degrees.

slides.heading: Effect of lone pairs on bond angles
slides.body_md: Methane, ammonia and water all have **four electron pairs** and a tetrahedral arrangement. Each lone pair **reduces the bond angle** because lone-pair repulsion is stronger than bond-pair repulsion.

visual.alt: Table of methane, ammonia and water with bond pairs, lone pairs, shape and bond angle decreasing with each lone pair

slides.narration: Compare three molecules that all have four electron pairs. Methane has none that are lone, and the angle is the ideal one hundred and nine and a half degrees. Ammonia has one lone pair, and the angle closes to one hundred and seven. Water has two, and the angle is only one hundred and four and a half degrees.

slides.heading: Shapes with lone pairs: ammonia, water and sulfur dioxide
slides.body_md: Take the **arrangement** from the total number of electron pairs, then name the **shape** from the atoms only. NH₃: tetrahedral arrangement, **trigonal pyramidal** shape. H₂O: tetrahedral arrangement, **bent**. SO₂: trigonal planar arrangement, **bent**.

slides.heading: Lone pairs on five and six pairs
slides.body_md: In a **trigonal bipyramid** lone pairs occupy **equatorial** positions (fewer 90° repulsions). In an **octahedron** the second lone pair goes **opposite** (trans to) the first.

visual.alt: Table of five species with their bond pairs, lone pairs, shape and hybridisation computed from the electron count

slides.narration: With five electron pairs, lone pairs go to the equatorial positions, where each has fewer close neighbours. One lone pair gives the see-saw shape of sulfur tetrafluoride, two give the T shape of chlorine trifluoride, and three give the straight line of xenon difluoride. With six pairs, one lone pair gives a square pyramid, and two opposite each other give a square plane.

slides.heading: Worked example: predicting shapes
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Predict the shape of $\ce{ICl2-}$, $\ce{H3O+}$ and $\ce{NH2-}$.

**Method.** Lone pairs on the central atom $= \dfrac{\text{valence electrons} - \text{bonds} - \text{charge}}{2}$.

**ICl₂⁻:** $(7 - 2 + 1)/2 = 3$ lone pairs, 2 bond pairs: linear, sp³d.

**H₃O⁺:** $(6 - 3 - 1)/2 = 1$: trigonal pyramidal, sp³.

**NH₂⁻:** $(5 - 2 + 1)/2 = 2$: bent, sp³.

slides.narration: Count the lone pairs on the central atom from its valence electrons, the number of bonds and the charge. The iodine ion has three lone pairs and two bonds, so it is linear. The hydronium ion has one lone pair and three bonds, so it is pyramidal like ammonia. The amide ion has two lone pairs and two bonds, so it is bent.

slides.body_md: A covalent bond forms by **overlap of half-filled orbitals**; the greater the overlap, the stronger the bond. **σ bonds** form by head-on overlap along the axis; **π bonds** by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals. A double bond is one σ and one π; a triple bond is one σ and two π.

slides.narration: Valence bond theory says a bond is formed when two half filled orbitals overlap. If the overlap is along the line joining the nuclei, we get a sigma bond. slides.heading: Hybridisation: sp, sp² and sp³
slides.body_md: **Hybridisation** mixes atomic orbitals of one atom to give **equivalent hybrid orbitals** with directional properties. Number of hybrid orbitals $=$ number of electron pairs (steric number).

visual.alt: Table of sp, sp2 and sp3 hybridisation with orbitals mixed, geometry, angle and examples

slides.narration: Hybridisation explains why methane has four equal bonds. The carbon s orbital mixes with three p orbitals to give four equivalent sp three hybrids pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. Mixing one s with two p gives three sp two hybrids in a plane, and one s with one p gives two sp hybrids on a line. The number of hybrids equals the number of electron pairs.

slides.heading: Hybridisation involving d orbitals
slides.body_md: **sp³d** (trigonal bipyramidal: PCl₅) and **sp³d²** (octahedral: SF₆) use **vacant d orbitals** of period 3 and later atoms. Lone pairs occupy hybrid orbitals too: SF₄ and ClF₃ are sp³d, BrF₅ and XeF₄ are sp³d².

visual.alt: Table of species with five or six electron pairs, their steric number, hybridisation and shape

slides.narration: Atoms in the third period and below have vacant d orbitals, so they can use them in hybridisation. Five pairs call for sp three d, with a trigonal bipyramid as the arrangement. Six pairs call for sp three d two, an octahedron. Remember to count lone pairs as well as bonds, so sulfur tetrafluoride is sp three d, and xenon tetrafluoride is sp three d two.

slides.heading: Worked example: hybridisation, sigma and pi bonds
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For ethene $\ce{C2H4}$, ethyne $\ce{C2H2}$ and $\ce{NH3}$, give the hybridisation of each central atom and count σ and π bonds.

**Ethene:** each C has 3 regions, so sp². Bonds: 4 C–H and 1 C–C σ, plus one π: **5σ + 1π**.

**Ethyne:** each C has 2 regions, so sp. Bonds: 2 C–H and 1 C–C σ, plus two π: **3σ + 2π**.

**Ammonia:** N has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair: 4 regions, sp³: **3σ**, no π.

visual.alt: Table of hybridisation and the number of sigma and pi bonds in ethene, ethyne and ammonia

slides.narration: Count the regions of electron density around each central atom: bonds, plus lone pairs, with a double or triple bond counted once. Ethene carbons have three regions and are sp two. Ethyne carbons have two and are sp. Ammonia nitrogen has four, counting its lone pair, so it is sp three. Then count sigma bonds first and add pi bonds for each extra bond.

slides.heading: Molecular orbital theory
slides.body_md: Atomic orbitals combine (**LCAO**) to form **molecular orbitals** over the whole molecule: **bonding** (lower energy, constructive) and **antibonding** (higher energy, destructive, marked *). Fill by **Aufbau**, **Pauli** and **Hund**. **Bond order = (Nb − Na)/2**. Unpaired electrons mean **paramagnetic**; none means **diamagnetic**.

visual.alt: Table of bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals and their effects

slides.narration: Molecular orbital theory treats electrons as belonging to the whole molecule. Two atomic orbitals combine to give a lower energy bonding orbital and a higher energy antibonding orbital. We fill the orbitals in order of energy, with Hund rule for equal ones. The bond order is the number of bonding electrons minus antibonding electrons, divided by two, and unpaired electrons mean the molecule is paramagnetic.

slides.heading: MO diagram of N₂: s–p mixing
slides.body_md: For **B₂, C₂ and N₂** the 2s and 2p orbitals are close in energy and **mix**, so **π2p lies below σ2p**. N₂ has 10 valence electrons: bond order **3**, no unpaired electrons, **diamagnetic**.

slides.narration: Oxygen has twelve valence electrons. Ten fill the same orbitals as in nitrogen, and the last two must go into the two degenerate antibonding pi orbitals. By Hund rule they go in one each, with parallel spins. So oxygen has two unpaired electrons and is attracted into a magnetic field, something Lewis structures could never explain.

slides.heading: Bond order and magnetism from H₂ to Ne₂
slides.body_md: Counting valence electrons (1s for H₂ and He₂) gives a bond order and magnetic behaviour for each homonuclear diatomic. **He₂, Be₂ and Ne₂** have bond order **0**: they do not exist as stable molecules.

visual.alt: Table of electrons, bond order, unpaired electrons and magnetic behaviour of the homonuclear diatomic molecules from hydrogen to neon

slides.narration: Apply the same filling to every molecule. Hydrogen has bond order one, helium zero, so the helium molecule does not exist. Boron has two unpaired electrons, because its last two electrons are in separate pi orbitals. Carbon has bond order two and no unpaired electrons. Nitrogen has three, oxygen two with unpaired electrons, fluorine one, and neon none.

slides.heading: Worked example: oxygen species
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Compare $\ce{O2+}$, $\ce{O2}$, $\ce{O2-}$ and $\ce{O2^2-}$ in bond order and magnetism.

Valence electrons: 11, 12, 13, 14. Fill σ2s, σ*2s, σ2p, π2p, π*2p:

- $\ce{O2+}$: (Nb − Na)/2 = 2.5, 1 unpaired.
- $\ce{O2}$: bond order 2, 2 unpaired.
- $\ce{O2-}$: bond order 1.5, 1 unpaired.
- $\ce{O2^2-}$: bond order 1, 0 unpaired (diamagnetic).

**Bond length** increases as the order falls: O₂⁺ < O₂ < O₂⁻ < O₂²⁻.

visual.alt: Table of the valence electrons, bond order and unpaired electrons of four oxygen species

slides.narration: Each extra electron goes into an antibonding pi orbital, so the bond order falls from two and a half in the positive ion, to two in oxygen, one and a half in superoxide, and one in peroxide. The bond gets longer along the series. Peroxide has all its electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic, while the others each have at least one unpaired electron.

slides.heading: Hydrogen bonding
slides.body_md: A **hydrogen bond** is the attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to **F, O or N** and a lone pair on another F, O or N atom. **Intermolecular** (between molecules): H₂O, HF, NH₃. **Intramolecular** (within one molecule): o-nitrophenol. It raises boiling points and makes ice **less dense** than water.

visual.alt: Table comparing the boiling points of water, hydrogen fluoride and ammonia with those of the hydrides of the next period

slides.narration: A hydrogen bond forms when hydrogen is attached to a very electronegative atom, fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, and is attracted to a lone pair on a neighbour. Water, hydrogen fluoride and ammonia boil far higher than their heavier relatives because of this. In o-nitrophenol the bond is inside the molecule, so it does not link molecules together and the compound is more volatile than the para isomer.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: VSEPR: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp; shape from atoms; SF₄ see-saw, ClF₃ T-shaped, XeF₂ linear, BrF₅ square pyramidal, XeF₄ square planar.
Valence bond theory: σ (head-on) and π (sideways) overlap; hybridisation sp, sp², sp³, sp³d, sp³d² from the steric number.
MO theory: bond order = (Nb − Na)/2; N₂ 3 (diamagnetic); O₂ 2 with two unpaired electrons (paramagnetic); π2p below σ2p only up to N₂.
Hydrogen bonds: intermolecular raise boiling points; intramolecular (o-nitrophenol) lower them.

visual.alt: Summary table of four models and what each explains

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. VSEPR gives shapes from electron pair repulsion, with lone pairs squeezing angles. Hybridisation and orbital overlap explain how bonds form in those shapes. Molecular orbital theory gives bond order and shows why oxygen is paramagnetic. And hydrogen bonds explain the unusually high boiling points of water, hydrogen fluoride and ammonia.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Show the count: bond pairs, lone pairs, then arrangement, then shape, then hybridisation.
Name the arrangement and the shape separately: NH₃ is tetrahedral in arrangement, pyramidal in shape.
For MO questions, write the electron configuration, then bond order and magnetic nature.
For N₂ and below (Z ≤ 7) use π2p before σ2p; for O₂ and F₂ use σ2p before π2p.
State whether a hydrogen bond is intermolecular or intramolecular, and its effect on boiling point or solubility.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. Count bond pairs and lone pairs before naming a shape, and keep arrangement and shape apart. For molecular orbital questions, write the configuration, then bond order, then magnetic nature, using the right order of orbitals. And for hydrogen bonding, say whether it is within a molecule or between molecules, and what that does to boiling point.

notes.title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Kössel–Lewis approach, ionic bonds and Lewis structures
sections.body_md:
Atoms combine to reach a noble-gas configuration: an **octet** (a duplet for H). A **Lewis symbol** shows valence electrons as dots. An **ionic bond** forms by electron transfer; it is favoured by a low ionisation enthalpy of the metal, a negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal and a high **lattice enthalpy**, which rises with higher ionic charge and smaller ionic size (NaCl about 788 kJ mol⁻¹; MgO about 3850 kJ mol⁻¹). A **covalent bond** is a shared pair.

**Lewis structure steps:** total valence electrons (adjust for charge); skeleton with the least electronegative atom central; single bonds; complete octets; add multiple bonds if electrons are short; check formal charges. **Exceptions:** incomplete octet (BeCl₂, BF₃), odd-electron (NO, NO₂), expanded octet (PCl₅, SF₆).

key_terms.definition_md: Atoms tend to have eight electrons in the outer shell.
Energy released when gaseous ions form one mole of the crystal.

sections.heading: 2. Formal charge
sections.body_md: **Formal charge = V − L − B/2.** In nitrate: N +1, double-bonded O 0, single-bonded O −1 (two), total −1. In ozone (O=O⁺–O⁻): central O +1, terminal O 0 and −1. The preferred structure has the smallest formal charges and puts any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

key_terms.definition_md: Valence electrons of the free atom minus non-bonding electrons minus half the bonding electrons.

sections.heading: 3. Bond parameters, resonance and polarity
sections.body_md:
**Bond length** (nuclear distance), **bond angle**, **bond enthalpy** (energy to break one mole of bonds in the gas phase) and **bond order**. For the same atoms: higher order, shorter and stronger (C–C 154 pm and 347 kJ mol⁻¹; C=C 134 and 611; C≡C 120 and 837). **Resonance:** the real structure is a hybrid; O₃ bond order 1.5, CO₃²⁻ and NO₃⁻ 1.33.

**Dipole moment** μ = q × d (debye; 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m), a vector. HF 1.78 D, HCl 1.07, HBr 0.79, HI 0.38. CO₂, BF₃, CH₄ and CCl₄ are non-polar by symmetry; H₂O 1.85 D; NH₃ 1.47 D, much more than NF₃ 0.23 D because in NF₃ the lone-pair dipole opposes the N–F dipoles.

key_terms.definition_md: Number of shared electron pairs between two atoms.
The real structure, a blend of the contributing Lewis structures.
Product of charge and distance of separation; a vector quantity.

sections.heading: 4. VSEPR theory
sections.body_md: Electron-pair regions repel: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair; a multiple bond is one region. Lone pairs lower bond angles (CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ 107°, H₂O 104.5°). In a trigonal bipyramid lone pairs go equatorial; in an octahedron the second lone pair goes trans to the first.

Number of bonded atoms plus lone pairs on the central atom.

sections.heading: 5. Valence bond theory and hybridisation
sections.body_md: A bond forms by overlap of half-filled orbitals. **σ** bonds: head-on overlap along the axis; **π** bonds: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals. A double bond = 1σ + 1π; a triple bond = 1σ + 2π. **Hybridisation** (number of hybrid orbitals = steric number): sp linear (BeCl₂, C₂H₂), sp² trigonal planar (BF₃, C₂H₄), sp³ tetrahedral (CH₄, NH₃, H₂O), sp³d trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅), sp³d² octahedral (SF₆). Ethene has 5σ + 1π; ethyne 3σ + 2π.

key_terms.definition_md: Bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the bond axis.
Bond formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals.
Mixing of atomic orbitals on one atom to form equivalent hybrid orbitals.

sections.heading: 6. Molecular orbital theory
sections.body_md: Atomic orbitals combine to give bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals. **Bond order = (Nb − Na)/2.** For Li₂ to N₂ the order is σ2s, σ*2s, π2p, σ2p, π*2p, σ*2p (s–p mixing); for O₂ and F₂, σ2p lies below π2p. N₂ has bond order 3 and is diamagnetic; O₂ has bond order 2 and two unpaired electrons (paramagnetic). O₂⁺ 2.5, O₂⁻ 1.5, O₂²⁻ 1.

Having unpaired electrons; attracted by a magnetic field.

sections.heading: 7. Hydrogen bonding
sections.body_md: H bonded to F, O or N attracts a lone pair on another F, O or N. **Intermolecular** H bonding (H₂O, HF, NH₃, alcohols) raises boiling points (H₂O 373 K, H₂S 213 K) and gives ice an open structure, so ice is less dense than water. **Intramolecular** H bonding (o-nitrophenol) keeps molecules separate, so the compound is more volatile (steam-volatile) than the para isomer.

key_terms.definition_md: Attraction between H bonded to F, O or N and a lone pair on another F, O or N.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Forgetting the lone pairs when counting steric number (XeF₄ is sp³d², not sp³).
- Giving NH₃ the shape “tetrahedral”; the arrangement is tetrahedral but the shape is trigonal pyramidal.
- Using σ2p below π2p for N₂ (mixing puts π2p lower) or the reverse for O₂.
- Saying CO₂ is non-polar because the C=O bonds are non-polar (the bonds are polar; the dipoles cancel).
- Writing the bond order of carbonate as 2 or 1 instead of 4/3.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a shape, a hybridisation, a bond order.
- 2–3 marks: count of pairs, then shape and reason.
- 5 marks: MO configuration, bond order, magnetic behaviour and a comparison.

questions.stem_md: In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, nitrogen has four single bonds and no lone pair. The formal charge on nitrogen is:
questions.solution_md: Formal charge = V − L − B/2 = 5 − 0 − 8/2 = +1 — option (b). Without the lone pair, nitrogen owns four electrons against five in the free atom.

questions.stem_md: In which molecule does the central atom have an incomplete octet?
questions.solution_md: Boron in BF₃ has only six electrons around it — option (d). N, C and O in the others each have eight.

questions.stem_md: Which of these ionic solids has the highest lattice enthalpy?
questions.solution_md: Lattice enthalpy rises with ionic charge and falls with ionic size. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges and are small, so MgO is highest — option (b). NaF (d) is next because of its small ions, but with single charges.

questions.stem_md: How many valence electrons must be shown in the Lewis structure of the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
questions.solution_md: Sulfur gives 6, each of four oxygens gives 6, and the two negative charges add 2: 6 + 24 + 2 = 32 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which species can have more than eight electrons around its central atom?
questions.solution_md: Sulfur is in period 3 and can use 3d orbitals, holding twelve electrons in SF₆ — option (c). Carbon and nitrogen (a, b) are in period 2 and have no d orbitals; boron (d) has an incomplete octet.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Phosphorus forms PCl₅ but nitrogen does not form NCl₅.

**Reason (R):** Nitrogen has vacant 3d orbitals that it uses to form three bonds only.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: nitrogen is in period 2 and has no d orbitals at all; this is why it cannot expand its octet — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? BF₃ has a non-zero dipole moment because each B–F bond is polar.
questions.solution_md: False. Each B–F bond is polar, but the molecule is trigonal planar, so the three bond dipoles cancel and the dipole moment is zero.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Intramolecular hydrogen bonding raises the boiling point of a compound by linking its molecules together.
questions.solution_md: False. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds form within one molecule and do not link molecules, so they make the compound more volatile; intermolecular bonds raise boiling points.

questions.stem_md: The number of lone pairs on the xenon atom in XeF₄ is ___.
questions.solution_md: Xenon has 8 valence electrons and four are used in bonds, leaving 2 lone pairs (**2**).

questions.stem_md: How many valence electrons are available for the Lewis structure of the phosphate ion, PO₄³⁻?
questions.solution_md: Phosphorus 5, four oxygens $4 \times 6$, and three for the charge: $5 + 4 \times 6 + 3 = 32$.

questions.stem_md: In the Lewis structure of ozone, O=O⁺–O⁻, the central oxygen has one lone pair and three bonds (six bonding electrons). What is its formal charge?
questions.solution_md: Formal charge $= V - L - B/2$, so $6 - 2 - 3 = 1$, that is +1.

questions.stem_md: Two Lewis structures are possible for CO₂: O=C=O and :O≡C–Ö:. Calculate the formal charges in each and say which is preferred.

answer.model_answer_md: In O=C=O every atom has formal charge zero. In the second structure carbon is 0, the triply bonded oxygen is +1 and the singly bonded oxygen is -1. O=C=O is preferred, having the smallest formal charges.

questions.solution_md: Compute V − L − B/2 for every atom in both structures.

questions.stem_md: Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.

answer.model_answer_md: Magnesium oxide contains doubly charged ions, Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, which are also small, so the electrostatic attraction in the crystal is much stronger. Its lattice enthalpy is several times that of sodium chloride, whose ions carry single charges and are larger, so far more energy is needed to break the lattice.

questions.solution_md: Higher charge and smaller ions give higher lattice enthalpy.

marking_scheme.step: Greater lattice enthalpy needs more energy to melt

questions.stem_md: Name three types of exception to the octet rule and give one example of each, with the number of electrons around the central atom.

answer.model_answer_md: In an incomplete octet the central atom has fewer than eight electrons, as boron in BF₃ with six. In an odd-electron molecule, such as NO₂, the central atom has an unpaired electron, so it cannot have an octet. In an expanded octet, a period 3 or later atom such as sulfur in SF₆ holds twelve electrons by using vacant d orbitals.

questions.solution_md: Incomplete, odd-electron and expanded octets with examples.

marking_scheme.step: Expanded octet with example and reason

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the steps for drawing the Lewis structure of a polyatomic ion.

(b) Draw the Lewis structure of the carbonate ion and calculate the formal charge on each atom.

(c) Why is the carbonate ion described by resonance structures, and what is the C–O bond order?

answer.model_answer_md: Count the valence electrons and add one for each negative charge, place the least electronegative atom in the centre, join atoms with single bonds, give octets, use multiple bonds if electrons are short, and check formal charges. Carbonate has 4 + 18 + 2 = 24 electrons; carbon forms one C=O and two C–O⁻ bonds. Formal charges are carbon 0, double-bonded oxygen 0 and each single-bonded oxygen -1, so the total is −2. The double bond can be placed on any of the three oxygens, giving three equivalent structures. The real ion is a hybrid with three equal C–O bonds of order 4/3, about 1.33.

questions.solution_md: Method; 24 electrons and formal charges; three equivalent structures and bond order 4/3.

questions.stem_md: The bond order of each N–O bond in the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, is:
questions.solution_md: One double and two single bonds are spread over three equivalent N–O bonds: (2 + 1 + 1)/3 = 1.33 — option (a). Ozone has bond order 1.5 (d).

questions.stem_md: Ammonia (1.47 D) and nitrogen trifluoride (0.23 D) are both pyramidal with a lone pair on nitrogen. The much smaller moment of NF₃ is because:

options.text_md: nitrogen has no lone pair in NF₃
the lone-pair dipole opposes the resultant of the N–F bond dipoles

questions.solution_md: In NF₃ fluorine is the negative end of each bond dipole, which points away from nitrogen, against the lone-pair dipole; in NH₃ both act in the same direction — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Arrange the C–C bond in ethane, ethene and ethyne in order of decreasing bond length.
questions.solution_md: Higher bond order gives a shorter bond: 154 pm (single), 134 pm (double), 120 pm (triple) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which bond has the highest bond enthalpy?
questions.solution_md: The triple bond of N₂ (946 kJ mol⁻¹) is far stronger than O=O (498), Cl–Cl (242) or F–F (159) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these molecules has zero dipole moment?
questions.solution_md: BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so its three bond dipoles cancel — option (a). The others are pyramidal, bent or have unequal bonds to carbon.

questions.stem_md: The H–X–H bond angles in CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O are 109.5°, 107° and 104.5°. The decrease is because:

options.text_md: lone pairs repel bond pairs more strongly than bond pairs repel each other

questions.solution_md: NH₃ has one lone pair and H₂O has two; the lone pair–bond pair repulsion squeezes the bond angle — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The two O–O bonds in ozone are equal in length.

**Reason (R):** The ozone molecule is bent.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the bent shape does not explain the equal bonds; resonance (a hybrid of two structures) does — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The dipole moment of NF₃ is much smaller than that of NH₃.

**Reason (R):** In NF₃ the lone-pair dipole opposes the N–F bond dipoles.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A: the opposing directions partly cancel in NF₃ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a resonance hybrid the molecule switches rapidly from one contributing structure to another.
questions.solution_md: False. The molecule has a single real structure, the hybrid, which is more stable than any contributing structure; the structures are only a way of describing it.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the bond order of each C–O bond in the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻.
questions.solution_md: One C=O and two C–O⁻ bonds are shared by three equivalent positions: $\dfrac{2 + 1 + 1}{3} = 1.33$.

questions.stem_md: The dipole moment of HF is 1.78 D and the H–F bond length is 92 pm. Calculate the percentage ionic character of the bond. (1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m; e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: Charge separated: $q = \dfrac{\mu}{d} = \dfrac{1.78 \times 3.336 \times 10^{-30}}{92 \times 10^{-12}} = 6.45 \times 10^{-20}$ C. Percentage ionic character: $\dfrac{6.45 \times 10^{-20}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} \times 100 = 40.3$, so about 40.3 per cent.

questions.stem_md: Use bond enthalpies (N≡N 946, H–H 436, N–H 391 kJ mol⁻¹) to estimate the enthalpy change, in kJ, for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g).
questions.solution_md: Bonds broken: 1 N≡N and 3 H–H; bonds formed: 6 N–H. $\Delta H = 946 + 3 \times 436 - 6 \times 391 = -92$, so $-92\ \text{kJ}$ for the reaction as written.

questions.stem_md: NH₃ has a dipole moment of 1.47 D while NF₃ has only 0.23 D, though N–F is more polar than N–H. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: In NH₃ nitrogen is the negative end of each N–H bond dipole, so the bond dipoles point towards nitrogen and add to the lone-pair dipole. In NF₃ fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen, so the bond dipoles point away from nitrogen and oppose the lone-pair dipole, giving a small resultant.

answer.model_answer_md: A hydrogen bond is the attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and a lone pair on another such atom. Association through intermolecular hydrogen bonds raises boiling points, so water (373 K) boils far above H₂S (213 K), and HF (293 K) above HCl (188 K).
